content.comment:
Interesting work. Happy to see more works in this direction.

But I would like to clarify two things about our iccv paper "pointcloud saliency maps" (mentioned in the introduction):
1. Although we only provide an informal proof on networks with a max-pooling layer (PointNet), this method is actually applicable to various network structures. This is because what we need to approximate the saliency map are only the gradients w.r.t. the radii.
2. Shifting points to the median is just an "imagined" differentiable operation (physical interpretation) to approximate the non-differentiable point dropping process. So in reality, we “did not” shift any points to the median to create pointy bumps but only approximated point-dropping by point-shifting, for the purpose of computing saliency maps of a standard point-cloud model for regular/incomplete point clouds "at the test time". Thus in the training stage, the model also does have to see any point clouds with pointy bumps. 

Anyway, this is an interesting paper to me.
Thanks,
Tianhang

content.review:
The paper proposes a method for morphing structured 3D shapes into a blob while keeping the basic relative structure between points. For example, in Figure 1(a). My confusion is why this is a real machine learning problem, despite the fact that papers are apparently being written about it at good conferences. For example, the quantitative measures being used are “internal” to the problem and seem to presuppose that this is useful, but it’s not clear if this helps do classification better or generate fake data better, or what? In general the paper is written well and the presentation is clear, but the problem doesn’t seem important to me.

Another concern is that the method seems only tangentially related to deep learning. The algorithm itself appears to be unrelated to deep learning, but can be run on the output of a deep learning model. Much of the idea is at the technical level of kernel smoothing (e.g., Eq 14), which is useful but very simple and not clearly an ICLR-type deep learning technical advance.

The paper is also proposed as an extension of a 2D visualization technique called I-GOS in Qi et al, (2019) to 3D in Section 3.2. Gradients apparently are more complicated in this higher dimensionality, which is addressed by Eq 14.

content.title: Response to Review
content.comment: The main concern from the reviewer seems to be whether the problem is important in practice. It needs to be kept in mind that although this paper spent a significant amount of space tackling the technical difficulty of smoothing the 3D point cloud, a main contribution is that it proposes a novel approach that visualizes which points/regions are utilized more in the prediction result of a point cloud network, while being agnostic to the type of point cloud network used. This can be used to debug/diagnose point cloud networks, gain insights to what the network is learning and potentially design better ones, as well as in certain difficult prediction tasks gain insights about what features are more discriminative on point clouds. We believe there would be broad interests on this topic, similar to the interest people have had in explaining CNNs in 2D images as in the classifier visualization related work that were cited in the paper.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
The paper proposes an algorithm to visualize the features learnt by 3D point cloud classifiers. The paper extends the I-GOS algorithms to point clouds. To enable the extension, the authors propose a novel algorithm to smooth point clouds which gradually smoothens the point cloud to a shape with a constant mean curvature. This is a first perturbation based algorithm for visualizing classifiers on point clouds. 

The proposed approach is experimentally validated on the smoothing capability of the novel point smoothing algorithm as well as the visualizations of point cloud networks using the extended I-GOS algorithm.  The results demonstrate that the proposed approach could be a practical and useful visualization tool for researchers working on point clouds as well as a good baseline for others to improve upon.

My main concern that the proposed approach seems ad hoc and the paper doesn’t establish the (formal) properties of the proposed approach. For example, it is not clear what sequence of smooth shapes will result from the smoothing algorithm and what the properties of that sequence will be. There are some other concerns about the writing clarity, technical material and inadequate discussions for the experimental results (see questions/ concerns below). 

Overall, however, the authors do propose a potentially useful point cloud visualization algorithm. If the authors can address the following concerns/ queries in their response and in the paper draft, I may be persuaded to revise my rating upwards.

Concerns/ Queries:

- Refer lines 92-103: “A close relative of visualization is adversarial attack”? The paragraph tries to shoehorn a comparison between visualizations and adversarial attacks which is irrelevant and distracting (tangential) to the objectives of this work. This should be appropriately rephrased. 

- What is anti-shrinkage? How is it defined? How are the proposed algorithms formally or empirically anti-shrinkage?

- What are the properties of the proposed smoothing algorithm? One way of thinking about point clouds is that a point cloud represents a shape on a differentiable manifold of shapes and the path between two shapes is represented by a geodesic. Then a smoothing operator may move the point cloud along the geodesic (shortest path) on the manifold of shape. In this vein, what are the properties of the proposed smoothing operator? What optimization problem is it a solution of?

- It seems that iterative smoothing gradually moves an informative shape to a non-informative shape in a sequence of steps. Is the final shape the same for all original shapes – a sphere (lines 270-272)? Does this property formally hold? If so, why the notion of ‘potatoes’ in the title? 

- In Figure 2, Taubin smoothing is shown to contain artifacts on a non-uniformly sampled ellipse. However, it is not clear if the sequence of shapes resulting from the application of the proposed smoothing algorithm in the right panel are ‘desirable’. Indeed, what properties should hold?

- It seems that the \phi operator makes the smoothing operation local, via a local mask M. Why should it be separately computed and not be a part of a single diffusion process which diffuses the local saliencies first and then operates more globally as the effective impact of a diffusion process spreads?

- Section 3.2 is not clear. The formulation in lines 204-209 implies that M is a solution to an optimization problem defined by the loss in (11). To compute that loss, the operator \phi needs to be defined which is implied to be done by (14). The eventual optimization problem to solve is never discussion, nor the difficulty and the nature of the solution. Finally, not providing a definition of \phi directly but just implying it causes confusion. I suggest that the authors make this section more clear. 

- Figs. 3 &4: It’ll be good to contrast these with results from the proposed algorithm.

- Table 1: The results for the DDS and MR metric should be discussed. What do the experiments show?

- Figure 5: How the color coding is done using the mask computed using the modified I-GOS algorithm in Figure 2 is not discussed and should be clarified. 

- In general, the authors should provide more explanations, discussions and takeaways for the conducted experiments.

content.title: Responses to the review
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer,

Thanks for your insightful and constructive feedback that helps to improve our paper. Our responses are listed below:

Q1: "This paper did not establish the (formal) properties of the proposed approach"

Ans: The goal of the smoothing is to smooth the approximated mean curvature among different points. The next revision would have Sec. 3.1 improved to reflect this.

Q2: "a comparison between visualizations and adversarial attacks is distracting"

Ans: This may be a subtle point, but the optimization problem solved by adversarial attacks and perturbation-based visualization are indeed  very similar, e.g. both tasks want to find the smallest set of points that can cause the classification score to drop the fastest if perturbed. Hence, these are important discussions rather than distractions. Especially, in perturbation-based visualization, one quick pitfall is to optimize the perturbation objective (e.g. eq.(13)) without enough smoothing terms, which would cause it to find adversarial masks and fail to discover meaningful patterns. The original I-GOS paper has some examples about this. Clarifications will be reflected in the new draft.

Q3: What is anti-shrinkage? How is it defined? How are the proposed algorithms formally or empirically anti-shrinkage?"

Ans: Anti-shrinkage is loosely defined as "the volume enclosed by the underlying manifold does not decrease as the algorithm iterates on the point cloud." To achieve this effect, we can either use Taubin's idea to "inflate" the shape by eq. 7, or we can manually normalize the size (i.e., the distances from the points to the origin) of the point cloud after each round of smoothing. In our experiments, we combined both strategies, and our algorithm is indeed empirically anti-shrinkage. Section 3.1 has been improved to describe this in terms of eigenvalues.

Q4: "Is the final shape the same for all original shapes – a sphere (lines 270-272)? Does this property formally hold? If so, why the notion of ‘potatoes’ in the title?"

Ans: Yes and no. Empirically, most of the shapes get morphed into a sphere as is promised by the property of curvature normal smoothing algorithm, but not always, because not all point clouds' underlying shape is a closed surface. The title will be changed in the new revision.

Q5: "Related to the ellipse figure. Indeed, what properties should hold?"

Ans: The mean curvature should be constant at every point after maximal smoothing.

Q6: "It seems that the \phi operator makes the smoothing operation local, via a local mask M. Why should it be separately computed and not be a part of a single diffusion process which diffuses the local saliencies first and then operates more globally as the effective impact of a diffusion process spreads?"

Ans: The goal is to obtain a differentiable version of \phi, as explained in Sec. 3.2. If enough intermediate shapes are used, the results shouldn't be very different from directly smoothing.

Q7: "Section 3.2 is not clear. The formulation in lines 204-209 implies that M is a solution to an optimization problem defined by the loss in (11). To compute that loss, the operator \phi needs to be defined which is implied to be done by (14). The eventual optimization problem to solve is never discussion, nor the difficulty and the nature of the solution. Finally, not providing a definition of \phi directly but just implying it causes confusion. I suggest that the authors make this section more clear. "

Ans: Thank you for pointing this out. Revision will be reflected in the new draft.

-"Figs. 3 &4: It’ll be good to contrast these with results from the proposed algorithm."

Ans: These figures will be added in the new draft.

-"Table 1: The results for the DDS and MR metric should be discussed. What do the experiments show?"


Ans: Revisions will be reflected in the new draft.


-"Figure 5: How the color coding is done using the mask computed using the modified I-GOS algorithm in Figure 2 is not discussed and should be clarified."

Ans: We added the color scheme to fig.5. Revisions will be reflected in the new draft.

-"In general, the authors should provide more explanations, discussions and takeaways for the conducted experiments."

Ans: We added more discussions for both the smoothing algorithm and the visualization algorithm. Revisions will be reflected in the new draft.

content.review:
This paper introduces an approach to realize the visualization of important features from point cloud networks. In order to see what parts are important to the point cloud classification, this approach smooth parts of the point cloud to remove certain shape features and evaluate the result on the original network. In addition, the author proves that the distance from the point to its local plane can represent the local curvature, which inspires them to find a proper way to smooth the shape.

I think the overall work is novel and interesting. But this paper also has some imprecise parts, here are a few:
1)	What is the motivation of using the constant mean curvature to smooth the point clouds?
2)	What is the value of β on the equation 11 in the experiments?
3)	There are some typing errors, e.g. “the a” in the 35th line. And the format of reference is nonstandard in line 405 to 406.

content.title: Responses to Review
content.comment:
Thanks for your constructive feedback. Our response to your concerns are listed below:

Q1: What is the motivation of using the constant mean curvature to smooth the point clouds?

Ans: Since we want to create a model-agnostic algorithm for visualizing point cloud classifiers, we are not allowed to simply delete points from the point cloud, which will make the point cloud different from the training distribution. Thus, we want to "blur away" some features of the point cloud while keeping it to look similar to a point cloud the algorithm has seen during training. With the key observation that edges and corners are just large curvature on the underlying surface, we specify the goal of our smoothing algorithm to be smoothing the mean curvature on the underlying surface of the point cloud. By smoothing out local curvature using mean curvature flow, we can identify which part of the shape is important to the network. The technical section of the paper will be improved in the next revision to discuss this.

Q2: What is the value of β on the equation 11 in the experiments?

Ans: We used 1 for β in our experiments. This'll be added to the next revision.

Q3: There are some typing errors, e.g. “the a” in the 35th line. And the format of reference is nonstandard in line 405 to 406.

Ans: These typos will be fixed in the next revision.

content.title: Official Blind Review #4
content.review:
This paper introduces an approach to compute the saliency map of a 3D point cloud, where the saliency is motivated from removing a region could result in a decrease in performance in shape classification. This idea was introduced in the image domain, and prior works leverage the so-called the natural neighborhood of image grids. However, such approaches do not naturally extend to 3D shapes, which are irregular, and particularly the 3D point cloud representation, which does not have well-defined connectivity information.  The basic idea of this approach is to apply variants Laplacian smoothing, which seeks to deform a shape to a sphere or a plane. This representation seeks to represent a pre-computed levelsets of masks, where each masked point is given by a linear combination of the corresponding points along this filtration (i.e., the weights of the combination depend on the mask value).

Although the proposed approach has a good motivation. It exhibits several technical issues.
1)	For images, when one sets the value of the mask to be zero, the corresponding pixel is 0. However, in the 3D representation, the ‘zero’ pixel is a point on a sphere, which does not vanish. It is unclear existing networks treat such regions the same way as convolution neural networks treat masked image regions.
2)	The smoothing operator can be quite unstable. A small region on the original shape could correspond a large region on the resulting sphere. The densities of the smoothed point cloud could change drastically (which is not an issue for images). Such issues appear quite often for spherical parameterizations of triangular meshes. They can get worse on point clouds. It would also be good to quantitively evaluate the performance of the resulting smoothed point clouds.
3)	The paper contains several adhoc parameters, such as 10 shapes for interpolation, switching spheres between planes (How to make such decisions for input point clouds that are like a half sphere?) 
4)	Another relevant question is how robust the proposed approach against a bad smoothing result is. Do the visualization results change?

In summary, although the motivation is good, the proposed approach is not convincing. The experimental results do not justify the robustness of the smoothing operator.

content.title: Response to Review
content.comment:
Thank you for your constructive feedback. We address your concerns below:

Q1: For images, when one sets the value of the mask to be zero, the corresponding pixel is 0. However, in the 3D representation, the ‘zero’ pixel is a point on a sphere, which does not vanish. It is unclear existing networks treat such regions the same way as convolution neural networks treat masked image regions.

Answer: Indeed this can be a limitation of the current algorithm. In the next revision we'll present the average prediction confidence on all the classes with the fully blurred point cloud. One can see that there are a few categories on ModelNet40 which tend to predict with significant confidence on a spherical point cloud, namely flower_pot, plant and vase. This means the current algorithm can't be reliably used on these 3 categories. In future work we would like to explore other notions of "featureless" on a point cloud to expand the use case.

Q2: The smoothing operator can be quite unstable. A small region on the original shape could correspond a large region on the resulting sphere. The densities of the smoothed point cloud could change drastically (which is not an issue for images). Such issues appear quite often for spherical parameterizations of triangular meshes. They can get worse on point clouds. It would also be good to quantitively evaluate the performance of the resulting smoothed point clouds.

Answer: Our quantitative evaluation result shows that the density distribution of the smoothed point cloud does not change much compared to the original point cloud. In the next revision we'll add density distribution similarity (DDS2) as an evaluation metric for the smoothing algorithms in sec 4.1 which directly addresses this concern.

Q3: The paper contains several adhoc parameters, such as 10 shapes for interpolation, switching spheres between planes (How to make such decisions for input point clouds that are like a half sphere?) 

Ans: The algorithm is not sensitive to the number of shapes used, hence we just put 10 there to balance accuracy and runtime. The other parameters are set to constant on the entire dataset to show that they are broadly applicable across many different shapes. In terms of the switching between spheres and planes, there is no decision that is made. As described in the paper, the planar version is always applied first, which does not change the point cloud much when the points do not lie on a plane since the estimated line will be very close to the point if it is not on the boundary. Then the spherical version is used afterwards. This was shown to empirically outperform another version which uses a threshold on plane fitting to determine planarity, and also eliminated one potential parameter.

Q4: Another relevant question is how robust the proposed approach against a bad smoothing result is. Do the visualization results change?

Ans: We will show some examples in the next revision.
